candidate.answerReason: The radicands are (sqrt(2)+1)^2 and (sqrt(2)-1)^2. Both binomials are positive, so their principal square roots differ by 2.

methods.label: Recognize perfect squares
methods.explanation:
The terms \(3\pm2\sqrt2\) suggest the perfect-square identity because \(3=2+1\). Indeed,
\[
(\sqrt2+1)^2=3+2\sqrt2,
\qquad
(\sqrt2-1)^2=3-2\sqrt2.
\]
A principal square root is nonnegative. Since \(\sqrt2>1\), both \(\sqrt2+1\) and \(\sqrt2-1\) are positive, so
\[
\sqrt{3+2\sqrt2}-\sqrt{3-2\sqrt2}
=(\sqrt2+1)-(\sqrt2-1)=2.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Recognizing binomial squares and choosing their nonnegative square roots uses elementary school algebra.

methods.label: Square the whole expression
methods.explanation:
Squaring the difference makes the two radicands add to \(6\), while their product simplifies by the difference-of-squares identity.

Let
\[
x=\sqrt{3+2\sqrt2}-\sqrt{3-2\sqrt2}.
\]
Both radicands are positive: \(3>2\sqrt2\) because their squares satisfy \(9>8\). The first radicand is larger, so \(x>0\). Expanding gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2
&=6-2\sqrt{(3+2\sqrt2)(3-2\sqrt2)}\\
&=6-2\sqrt{9-8}=4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(x>0\), we take the positive root and obtain \(\boxed{x=2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
methods.levelReason: Squaring a binomial and multiplying nonnegative square roots are elementary algebra; the sign check selects the correct root.
